name: Sacsayhuamán
info: Sacsayhuamán is the Inca citadel on the hill above Cusco, Peru, built in the 15th century in dry stone walls of huge cut blocks, later stripped by the Spaniards for building stone and now listed with Cusco by UNESCO.

facts.made: Built by the Inca; Inca oral history, as the Spanish chroniclers recorded it, places the work in the reigns of Pachacuti, Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac, with labour supplied by the provinces
facts.form: A fortified ceremonial complex on a steep hill at 3,701 metres, with a great plaza and three massive terrace walls of dry stone, the longest about 400 metres long and about 6 metres tall
facts.where: On the northern outskirts of Cusco, Peru, the historic capital of the Inca Empire
facts.known: walls of huge limestone blocks cut to fit without mortar; the great plaza; the lion-shaped plan of Cusco, with the fortress as its head; the Spanish quarrying of the site; the festivals of Inti Raymi and Warachikuy held there

t: Inca oral history, recorded by Spanish chroniclers, says the fortress was built under Pachacuti and his successors Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac, to serve as the head of the lion-shaped city of Cusco.

Its terrace walls use some of the largest stones in pre-Hispanic America, set without mortar; the largest limestone block is estimated at 128 tonnes to almost 200 tonnes and was moved an estimated 35 km from Rumicolca.
After the siege of Cusco the Spaniards pulled down much of the complex for building stone, so that today mostly the blocks too large to move remain.
dyk: Pedro Cieza de León wrote in 1553 that the Inca had the provinces supply 20,000 men for the work, of whom 4,000 quarried the stone and 6,000 hauled it with great cables of leather and cabuya.
ev: The earliest occupation of the hilltop, as indicated by surface collections of pottery
The Imperial Inca expanded the settlement with dry stone walls of huge stones
Pedro Cieza de León wrote his account of the fortress and of its pillaging by the Spaniards

Archaeologists found further ruins at the periphery of the site

sections.origins:
Sacsayhuamán, or Saksaywaman, is a citadel on the northern outskirts of the city of Cusco, Peru, the historic capital of the Inca Empire. It stands on a steep hill that overlooks the city, at an altitude of 3,701 metres, with a wide view of the valley to the southeast. The name comes from the Quechua Saksay waman pukara, 'fortress of the royal falcon or hawk'. Surface collections of pottery indicate that the earliest occupation of the hilltop dates to about 900 CE, and it has been theorised that the site was first built upon during the Killke period, which preceded the Inca.

The Spanish chroniclers recorded that, in Inca oral history, the fortress was built during the reign of the Sapa Inca Pachacuti and his successors, Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac. According to that history, Túpac Inca remembered that his father Pachacuti had called Cuzco the lion city, its tail where the two rivers unite, its body the great square and the houses round it, and its head wanting. The Inca decided that the best head would be a fortress on a high plateau to the north of the city. During the 15th century the Imperial Inca expanded on the existing settlement, building dry stone walls of huge stones.
sections.content:
The best-known zone of Sacsayhuamán includes its great plaza and its adjacent three massive terrace walls. The longest of the three walls is about 400 metres, and they are about 6 metres tall. The stones are among the largest used in any building in pre-Hispanic America and display a precision of cutting and fitting that is unmatched in the Americas: many of them are so closely spaced that a single piece of paper will not fit between them. This precision, together with the rounded corners of the blocks, the variety of their interlocking shapes and the way the walls lean inward, is thought to have helped the ruins survive devastating earthquakes in Cuzco.

The large plaza, capable of holding thousands of people, was designed for communal ceremonial activities, and several of the large structures at the site may also have been used in rituals. Pedro Pizarro, who saw the fortress when the Spaniards entered Cusco, described a very strong fort with masonry walls, two very high round towers and a hillside built up in terraces and flat spaces. He recorded rooms filled with arms, lances, arrows, clubs and shields, and described storage rooms for military equipment. Cieza de León, for his part, wrote of many buildings within the fortress, some small and one above another, and larger ones underground, in two blocks, one larger than the other. He recorded that the natives called it the House of the Sun.
sections.making:
Cieza de León, writing in 1553, recorded that the Inca ordered the provinces to provide 20,000 men and the villages to send provisions. A sick man was replaced by another, and the labourers were relieved after a limited time by others. Of the men, 4,000 quarried and cut the stones, and 6,000 conveyed them to the works with great cables of leather and cabuya; the rest opened the ground, prepared the foundations and cut posts and beams for the woodwork. The labourers made their dwelling huts near the works, each lineage apart, under overseers and great masters of the art of building. Cieza wrote that the work was commenced in the time of Ynca Yupanqui and that his son Tupac Inca, Huayna Ccapac and Huascar worked much at it.

The walls were built of dry stone, the blocks carefully cut to fit together tightly without mortar. The estimated volume of stone is over 6,000 cubic metres, and the weight of the largest limestone block is estimated at between 128 tonnes and almost 200 tonnes. The stones were moved an estimated 35 km (22 miles) from Rumicolca. How the blocks were set is a matter of theory. Vince Lee proposed that they were carved first and then lowered into prepared pockets in the wall, towed up a ramp and eased down on a stack of logs removed one at a time. His experiments with this method, and with towing large stones at Ollantaytambo, had limited success and could not replicate what Cieza claimed to have seen; the largest megaliths now at the site are more than twice the size of the largest Cieza estimated in his time.
sections.reception:
The Spaniards who saw the fortress wrote of it with wonder. Cieza de León, who said he went to see it twice and related nothing he had not seen, wrote that the walls were so strong that no artillery could breach them and that the stones were laid with such delicacy that a rial could not be put between two of them. Some of the stones, he wrote, were twelve feet wide and more than twenty long, so large that it tired the judgment to conceive how they were conveyed and placed. Near the fortress he saw a stone of 260 palmos in circuit, of which, he reported, the Indians said that it got tired at that point and they could not move it further. He judged the fortress still worthy of admiration, though formerly without comparison grander.

Pedro Pizarro likewise wrote that the lowest stones were so large and thick that it seemed impossible that human hands had set them in place, and so well fitted that the point of a pin could not be inserted in the joints. Cieza also complained that the Spaniards had so pillaged and ruined the work that he would be sorry to have been guilty of the fault of those in power who permitted it. He urged that what was left be preserved and given a guard, as a memorial of the grandeur of the Inca.
sections.survival:
Following the siege of Cusco, the Spaniards began to use Sacsayhuamán as a source of stones for building Spanish Cuzco. Within a few years they had taken apart and demolished much of the complex, block by block, to salvage materials for the new Spanish governmental and religious buildings of the colonial city and the houses of its wealthiest Spaniards. Garcilaso de la Vega wrote, in 1609, that to save themselves the expense, effort and delay with which the Indians worked the stone, the Spaniards pulled down all the smooth masonry in the walls, and that there was not a house in the city that had not been made of this stone, or at least the houses built by the Spaniards.

Today it is mostly the pre-colonial stones too large to be easily moved that remain at the site. In modern times upper retaining walls were added to some sections as erosion control. These rougher-fitting walls are missing in photographs from the early 1900s, and some of them have modern dates etched on them. In 1983 Cusco and Sacsayhuamán together were designated as sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, for international recognition and protection. On 13 March 2008 archaeologists discovered additional ruins at the periphery of the site; they appear ceremonial, but their exact function remains unknown. In January 2010 parts of the site were damaged during heavy rainfall in the region.
sections.legacy:
Sacsayhuamán is regarded as an important example of Inca architecture, and the walls of its terraces are the best-known surviving part of the work. Its place in the plan of Cusco, as the head of the lion that Pachacuti was said to have seen in the city, gave the Inca capital a form that the Spanish town grew over. The Inca repeated a similar relationship between a city and a fortress in a distant colony, where Santiago, Chile, later developed: the Inca fortress there, known as Chena, predated the Spanish colonial city and was a ceremonial ritual site, the Huaca de Chena.

The site is still used for ceremony. Peruvians continue to celebrate Inti Raymi, the annual Inca festival of the winter solstice and new year, which is held near Sacsayhuamán on 24 June. Another important festival, Warachikuy, is held there each year on the third Sunday of September. Some people from Cusco also use the large field within the walls for jogging, tai chi and other athletic activities. How the great blocks were moved and set has also been tested by experiment, with limited success, in work led by Vince Lee at Ollantaytambo.

summary: Sacsayhuamán is the Inca citadel above Cusco, built in the 15th century with dry stone terrace walls of huge cut blocks. The Spaniards quarried much of it for colonial Cusco after the siege of the city, and the large stones that remain were listed with Cusco by UNESCO in 1983.
notes: Start: the article gives no single year, only the 15th century for the Imperial Inca building; 1400 used with circa true. The article also says earliest occupation about 900 CE and a possible Killke-period first building.

Attribution of the fortress differs inside the article: the lead and oral history name Pachacuti, Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac; Cieza names Ynca Yupanqui, Tupac Inca, Huayna Ccapac and Huascar. Both are given with their sources.

Cieza's figures (20,000 men, 330 by 200 paces) are his own; stone weights vary (128 tonnes to almost 200 tonnes). The article says Vince Lee's experiments could not match Cieza's claims and that the largest blocks are more than twice his estimates; the saved text breaks off a line there, which was read as continuing.
The article's 'Pedro Pizarro' passage about Coricancha's gold plates is about Cusco's Temple of the Sun, not this site, and was left out.
Tourism and the external links were left out.
